speaker: periodista
text: Good afternoon and welcome to our press conference with President Lagarde and Vice-President de Guindos.

speaker: periodista
text: My name is Wolfgang Preussl. We have also participants that are connected via video stream.

speaker: periodista
text: If they take the floor and ask questions, I would ask them to turn on the camera and the microphones, obviously.

speaker: periodista
text: And with that, I hand over to President Lagarde, please.

speaker: presidenta
text: Thank you very much, Volgong, and good afternoon to all of you present in the room and on screen.

speaker: presidenta
text: So the Vice President and I welcome you to our press conference.

speaker: presidenta
text: We would like to begin by congratulating Bulgaria on joining the Euro Area on January 1, 2026. We also warmly welcome Dimitar Radev, the governor of the Bulgarian National Bank.

speaker: presidenta
text: He joined the governing council today with voting capacity.

speaker: presidenta
text: Membership of the euro area has almost doubled since 1999

speaker: presidenta
text: and is testimony to the attractiveness of the single currency

speaker: presidenta
text: and the enduring benefits of European integration.

speaker: presidenta
text: We will now report on the outcome of today's meeting. The Governing Council today decided to keep the three key ECB interest rates unchanged.

speaker: presidenta
text: Our updated assessment reconfirms that inflation should stabilize at our 2% target in the medium

speaker: presidenta
text: term.

speaker: presidenta
text: The economy remains resilient in a challenging global environment.

speaker: presidenta
text: Low unemployment, solid private sector balance sheets, the gradual rollout of public spending

speaker: presidenta
text: on defence and infrastructure, and the supportive effects of our past interest rate cuts are

speaker: presidenta
text: underpinning growth.

speaker: presidenta
text: At the same time, the outlook is still uncertain, owing particularly to ongoing global trade

speaker: presidenta
text: policy uncertainty and geopolitical tensions.

speaker: presidenta
text: We are determined to ensure that inflation stabilizes at our 2 percent target in the

speaker: presidenta
text: medium term.

speaker: presidenta
text: We will follow a data-dependent and meeting-by-meeting approach to determining the appropriate monetary

speaker: presidenta
text: policy stance. In particular, our interest rate decisions will be based on our assessment

speaker: presidenta
text: of the inflation outlook and the risks surrounding it, in light of the incoming economic and

speaker: presidenta
text: financial data, as well as the dynamics of underlying inflation and the strength of monetary

speaker: presidenta
text: policy transmission. We are not pre-committing to a particular rate path.

speaker: presidenta
text: The decisions taken today are set out in a press release available on our website.

speaker: presidenta
text: And I will now outline in more detail how we see the economy and inflation developing,

speaker: presidenta
text: and will then explain our assessment of financial and monetary conditions.

speaker: presidenta
text: So looking at the economic activity first.

speaker: presidenta
text: The economy grew by 0.3% in the fourth quarter of 2025, according to Eurostat's preliminary

speaker: presidenta
text: flash estimate.

speaker: presidenta
text: Growth has mainly been driven by services, notably in the information and communication

speaker: presidenta
text: sector.

speaker: presidenta
text: Manufacturing has been resilient despite the headwinds from global trade and geopolitical

speaker: presidenta
text: uncertainty.

speaker: presidenta
text: system in construction is picking up, also supported by public investment.

speaker: presidenta
text: The labour market continues to support incomes, even though demand for labour has cooled further.

speaker: presidenta
text: Unemployment stood at 6.2% in December, after 6.3% in November.

speaker: presidenta
text: Increasing labor incomes, together with a lower household saving rate, should bolster

speaker: presidenta
text: private consumption.

speaker: presidenta
text: Government spending on defense and infrastructure should also contribute to domestic demand.

speaker: presidenta
text: Business investment should strengthen further, and surveys indicate that firms are increasingly

speaker: presidenta
text: investing in new digital technologies.

speaker: presidenta
text: At the same time, the external environment remains challenging, owing to higher tariffs

speaker: presidenta
text: and a stronger euro over the past year.

speaker: presidenta
text: The Governing Council stresses the urgent need to strengthen the euro area and its economy

speaker: presidenta
text: in the present geopolitical context.

speaker: presidenta
text: should prioritize sustainable public finances, strategic investment, and growth-enhancing

speaker: presidenta
text: structural reforms. Unlocking the full potential of the single market remains crucial. It is

speaker: presidenta
text: also vital to foster greater capital market integration by completing the Savings and

speaker: presidenta
text: Investments Union and the Banking Union to an ambitious timetable, and to rapidly adopt

speaker: presidenta
text: the regulation on the establishment of the digital euro.

speaker: presidenta
text: Looking now at inflation.

speaker: presidenta
text: Inflation declined to 1.7 percent in January from 2 percent in December and 2.1 percent

speaker: presidenta
text: in November.

speaker: presidenta
text: Energy inflation dropped to minus 4.1% after minus 1.9% in December and 0.5% in November,

speaker: presidenta
text: while food price inflation increased to 2.7% from 2.5% in December and 2.4% in November.

speaker: presidenta
text: Inflation excluding energy and food eased to 2.2% after 2.3% in December and 2.4% in

speaker: presidenta
text: November.

speaker: presidenta
text: Goods inflation edged up to 0.4%, whereas services inflation declined to 3.2% from 3.4%

speaker: presidenta
text: December and 3.5 percent in November. Indicators of underlying inflation have

speaker: presidenta
text: changed little over recent months and remain consistent with our 2 percent

speaker: presidenta
text: medium-term target. Negotiated wage growth and forward-looking indicators,

speaker: presidenta
text: such as the ECB's wage tracker and surveys on wage expectations, point to

speaker: presidenta
text: continued moderation in labor costs. However, the contribution to overall wage

speaker: presidenta
text: growth from payment over and above the negotiated wage component remains

speaker: presidenta
text: uncertain. Most measures of longer-term inflation expectations continue to stand

speaker: presidenta
text: at around 2%, supporting the stabilization of inflation around our

speaker: presidenta
text: target. On the risk, the euro area continues to face a volatile global

speaker: presidenta
text: policy environment. A renewed increase in uncertainty could weigh on demand. A

speaker: presidenta
text: deterioration in global financial market sentiment could also dampen demand.

speaker: presidenta
text: Further frictions in international trade could disrupt supply chains, reduce exports, and weaken consumption and investment.

speaker: presidenta
text: Geopolitical tensions, in particular Russia's unjustified war against Ukraine, remain a major source of uncertainty.

speaker: presidenta
text: By contrast, planned defence and infrastructure spending, together with the adoption of productivity-enhancing reforms and the adoption of new technologies by euro-area firms, may drive up growth by

speaker: presidenta
text: more than expected, including through positive effects on business and consumer confidence.

speaker: presidenta
text: New trade agreements and a deeper integration of our European single market could also boost

speaker: presidenta
text: growth beyond current expectations.

speaker: presidenta
text: The outlook for inflation continues to be more uncertain than usual on account of the

speaker: presidenta
text: volatile global policy environment.

speaker: presidenta
text: Inflation could turn out to be lower if tariffs reduce demand for Euro-area exports by more

speaker: presidenta
text: than expected, and if countries with overcapacity increase further their exports to the euro

speaker: presidenta
text: area.

speaker: presidenta
text: Moreover, a stronger euro could bring inflation down beyond current expectations.

speaker: presidenta
text: More volatile and risk-averse financial markets could weigh on demand and thereby also lower

speaker: presidenta
text: inflation.

speaker: presidenta
text: By contrast, inflation could turn out to be higher if there were a persistent upward shift

speaker: presidenta
text: in energy prices or if more fragmented global supply chains pushed up import prices, curtailed

speaker: presidenta
text: the supply of critical raw materials and added to capacity constraints in the euro-area economy.

speaker: presidenta
text: If wage growth moderated more slowly, services inflation might come down later than expected.

speaker: presidenta
text: The planned boost in defence and infrastructure spending could also cause inflation to pick

speaker: presidenta
text: up over the medium term.

speaker: presidenta
text: And extreme weather events and the unfolding climate and nature crisis more broadly could

speaker: presidenta
text: drive up food prices by more than expected.

speaker: presidenta
text: So looking at financial and monetary conditions.

speaker: presidenta
text: Market rates have come down since our last meeting, while global trade and geopolitical

speaker: presidenta
text: tensions temporarily increased financial market volatility.

speaker: presidenta
text: Bank lending rates for firms ticked up to 3.6% in December from 3.5% in November, as

speaker: presidenta
text: did the cost of issuing market-based debt.

speaker: presidenta
text: The average interest rate on new mortgages again held steady at 3.3% in December.

speaker: presidenta
text: Bank lending to firms grew by 3% on a yearly basis in December, after 3.1% in November

speaker: presidenta
text: and 2.9% in October.

speaker: presidenta
text: The issuance of corporate bonds rose by 3.4% in December.

speaker: presidenta
text: According to our latest bank lending survey for euro-area firms, demand for credit was

speaker: presidenta
text: up slightly in the fourth quarter, especially to finance inventories and working capital.

speaker: presidenta
text: At the same time, credit standards for business loans tightened again.

speaker: presidenta
text: Mortgage lending grew by 3% after 2.9% in November and 2.8% in October, in response

speaker: presidenta
text: to still rising demand for loans and an easing of credit standards.

speaker: presidenta
text: So to conclude, the Governing Council today decided to keep the three key ECB interest

speaker: presidenta
text: rates unchanged.

speaker: presidenta
text: We are determined to ensure that inflation stabilizes at our 2% target in the medium

speaker: presidenta
text: term.

speaker: presidenta
text: We will follow a data-dependent and meeting-by-meeting approach to determining the appropriate monetary

speaker: presidenta
text: policy stance. Our interest rate decisions will be based on our assessment of the inflation

speaker: presidenta
text: outlook and the risks surrounding it, in light of the incoming economic and financial data

speaker: presidenta
text: as well as the dynamics of underlying inflation and the strength of monetary policy transmission.

speaker: presidenta
text: We are not pre-committing to a particular rate path. And in any case, we stand ready

speaker: presidenta
text: to adjust all of our instruments within our mandate, to ensure that inflation stabilizes

speaker: presidenta
text: sustainably at our medium-term target, and to preserve the smooth functioning of monetary

speaker: presidenta
text: policy transmission. And we are now ready to take your questions.

speaker: periodista
text: The first question goes to Alex Weber of Bloomberg. Alex, please.

speaker: periodista
text: Thank you very much. Good afternoon. My first question is on the risk assessment.

speaker: periodista
text: the events of recent weeks including new tariff threats by the US. Would you say that inflation

speaker: periodista
text: and economic risks on both sides have become more pronounced again and has the ECB's good place

speaker: periodista
text: perhaps become a little less comfortable? And then I'm also curious how you discussed

speaker: periodista
text: the euro's exchange rate this week during your meeting. Has the recent appreciation

speaker: periodista
text: against the dollar perhaps increased any concerns in the governing council that

speaker: periodista
text: that inflation might turn out lower than expected?

speaker: presidenta
text: Well, thank you for your two questions.

speaker: presidenta
text: Let me first of all mention to all of you

speaker: presidenta
text: that the Governing Council took a unanimous decision

speaker: presidenta
text: to keep the rates at their current level unchanged.

speaker: presidenta
text: In relation to our risk assessment, you will have seen that we take a one-hand-the-other-hand approach, both in relation to activity and in relation to inflation.

speaker: presidenta
text: And if you look at the balancing act between the two, we are, as I would call it, in a broadly

speaker: presidenta
text: balanced situation when it comes to risk assessment.

speaker: presidenta
text: And some risks have ticked up, others have ticked down.

speaker: presidenta
text: But on balance, taking the various specific elements that we make sure we list in a rather

speaker: presidenta
text: exhaustive way, we believe that we are in a broadly balanced situation at the moment.

speaker: presidenta
text: So on the exchange rate, because I know that this is a question that has been on the mind

speaker: presidenta
text: of some. I just want to remind you, and this will not come as a surprise, that we do not

speaker: presidenta
text: target an exchange rate in terms of policy target. But we also recognise that it is important

speaker: presidenta
text: for growth and inflation outlook, both. So, for that reason, we always keep a close eye

speaker: presidenta
text: on exchange rate developments,

speaker: presidenta
text: and the Governing Council discussed this matter today.

speaker: presidenta
text: Now, what we observed collectively

speaker: presidenta
text: is that the dollar has depreciated measurably

speaker: presidenta
text: against the euro, but not in the last few days,

speaker: presidenta
text: but since March 2025.

speaker: presidenta
text: That's when you see the significant change at the time.

speaker: presidenta
text: And in the last few weeks, actually since the summer, it has fluctuated within a range. And whether you look at the Euro-US dollar, whether you look at nominal effective exchange

speaker: presidenta
text: rate, the story is the same.

speaker: presidenta
text: So as a result of that observation, we concluded that the impact of exchange rate appreciation

speaker: presidenta
text: since last year is incorporated in our baseline, OK?

speaker: presidenta
text: But of course, as I said, we always monitor whether the impact is passing through as expected

speaker: presidenta
text: and how it affects our reaction function.

speaker: presidenta
text: That's the analysis that we conducted.

speaker: presidenta
text: So it's a topic that we touched, that we explored, and our conclusion is as I have just described.

speaker: presidenta
text: I would also observe that the current range

speaker: presidenta
text: within which the euro relative to the dollar is evolving

speaker: presidenta
text: is very much in line with the overall average

speaker: presidenta
text: of that exchange rate between the euro and the dollar

speaker: presidenta
text: for as long as the euro has been around.

speaker: periodista
text: Next question for Annette Weisbach of CNBC.

speaker: periodista
text: Annette, please.

speaker: vicepresidente
text: President Lagarde, I have two questions.

speaker: vicepresidente
text: A, on the role of the global euro.

speaker: vicepresidente
text: Global euro, you wanted to push the importance of the euro globally, don't you have to take into account then also a stronger euro towards the rest of the world? My first question.

speaker: vicepresidente
text: Second question is, there are reports that you're looking into repurpose in the swap lines,

speaker: vicepresidente
text: so enlarging the liquidity pool which is available of euro also beyond its current

speaker: vicepresidente
text: purpose in order to also enlarge the importance of the euro. So perhaps you can tell us a little bit more about those plans, also in light of the fact that the independence of the Fed

speaker: vicepresidente
text: is actually currently questioned by the markets. Thank you.

speaker: presidenta
text: So your first question, thank you very much for both. Your first question has to do with the

speaker: presidenta
text: the international role of the euro, and it is a point that I made about a year ago

speaker: presidenta
text: and that we collectively as governing council feel strongly about.

speaker: presidenta
text: Second observation, it is not because you have an international currency

speaker: presidenta
text: that plays a global role that it necessarily implies that it is

speaker: presidenta
text: quote, strong, unquote, relative to others.

speaker: presidenta
text: There is currently a currency which is playing that role,

speaker: presidenta
text: but it does not necessarily come together with a currency being, as a result, strong.

speaker: presidenta
text: There is no fatality, if you will, or correlation between the two,

speaker: presidenta
text: being a strong international currency and being appreciated relative to other currencies.

speaker: presidenta
text: So, first observation.

speaker: presidenta
text: Second observation, I have said in the past in that speech which I think I gave in Berlin, if I recall,

speaker: presidenta
text: that for a currency to play an international global role

speaker: presidenta
text: and to be powerful as a result requires a few other elements

speaker: presidenta
text: that build over the course of time.

speaker: presidenta
text: And it clearly goes with a reliable environment, a safe environment, where the rule of law is known and respected.

speaker: presidenta
text: I have no doubt about that particular aspect as far as the euro and the euro area is concerned.

speaker: presidenta
text: It requires a strong position relative to the rest of the world.

speaker: presidenta
text: And there are clearly investments that are flagged in our monetary policy statement, and particularly in relation to defence and infrastructure that go in that direction,

speaker: presidenta
text: but where clearly work has to be done.

speaker: presidenta
text: There is a third component which is also improving and has continued to improve recently,

speaker: presidenta
text: which is the capacity to trade with the rest of the world.

speaker: presidenta
text: And I would regard both the Mercosur, the EU-India trade agreement,

speaker: presidenta
text: subsequent trade agreements in Australia and other corners of the world

speaker: presidenta
text: where the Commission is doing hard work as other components

speaker: presidenta
text: that are necessary for the currency to be strong.

speaker: presidenta
text: So, yes, not necessarily aligned with an appreciation of the currency.

speaker: presidenta
text: And three, more work needs to be done in those various directions.

speaker: presidenta
text: One of the attributes of a strong currency is to be the provider of liquidity.

speaker: presidenta
text: And while we are tied to the monetary purpose of what we do in terms of liquidity and we have to constantly assess the proportionality of what we do, it is a fact that we are looking at our liquidity framework and that the repo line, to be distinguished from the swap lines, The repo line are in progress in terms of reframing them, opening up the access and making them more attractive to other national central banks outside the euro area and outside Europe.

speaker: presidenta
text: So this is in the works and I hope to be able to announce a bit more in a few days.

speaker: presidenta
text: Thank you.

speaker: periodista
text: Next question to Francesco Canepa of Reuters.

speaker: periodista
text: Francesco, please.
Good afternoon.
So my first question is about the balance of risk.
You said it's broadly balanced.
Could you give us some of the flavor of the discussion?
Because I don't see it in the opening statement.
And the second question is about the good place.
Are we still in a good place?

speaker: presidenta
text: Thank you. Thank you very much. You will have noted, because you are an avid reader of our monetary policy statement, that we no longer state in the monetary policy statement whether the balance of risk is broadly, whether the risks are broadly balanced or tilted to the downside or tilted to the upside. We did that during the period of COVID because we thought it was good guidance to have at the time.

speaker: presidenta
text: Now what we do as a policy and as a general practice that we have not moved since COVID is we list the upside and the downside risks component, both in relation to growth and in relation to inflation.

speaker: presidenta
text: And then it's not for you to actually second guess. There is a debate that goes on in the governing council

speaker: presidenta
text: because it's always a question of judgment

speaker: presidenta
text: and collective approach to those risks

speaker: presidenta
text: and the range of the risks,

speaker: presidenta
text: the extensiveness of the risks,

speaker: presidenta
text: and that is debated.

speaker: presidenta
text: What I can tell you is that

speaker: presidenta
text: we are not seeing a reduction of the range of risks.

speaker: presidenta
text: But, you know, when I think of geopolitical risks, for instance,

speaker: presidenta
text: it's ebb and flow.

speaker: presidenta
text: When I look at uncertainty about tariffs,

speaker: presidenta
text: it's up and down and out and back.

speaker: presidenta
text: And that has been going on for quite a few quarters, actually.

speaker: presidenta
text: So, no reduction of the range,

speaker: presidenta
text: but equally the sentiment around the table of the governing council that it's broadly balanced.

speaker: presidenta
text: Now, are we still in a good place?

speaker: presidenta
text: I would certainly argue that we are in a good place and inflation is in a good place. Now, two words of explanation because some of you might be riveted to the January data point

speaker: presidenta
text: And I would like just to remind you that our good place is a factor of whether we are convinced that we will reach our medium-term target of 2%.

speaker: presidenta
text: And we cannot be hostage to one data point.

speaker: presidenta
text: I've said that many times.

speaker: presidenta
text: We cannot be hostage to one reading of inflation, which is set to vary over the next months.

speaker: presidenta
text: If you look at, I'm happy to go down into what's underneath,

speaker: presidenta
text: but this 1.7, there are multiple causes,

speaker: presidenta
text: and in the monetary policy statement,

speaker: presidenta
text: we take really good care of saying what has gone up, what has gone down. You have a bit more of one category versus the others,

speaker: presidenta
text: so as a result of that, we have this particular reading.

speaker: presidenta
text: But some of them are idiosyncratic and will go away.

speaker: presidenta
text: There is a significant component on energy, which has gone from minus 5 point something,

speaker: presidenta
text: sorry, which has gone to minus 5 point something,

speaker: presidenta
text: and which is largely a base effect from last year's energy costs.

speaker: presidenta
text: But it is also a fact that inflation is moving gradually down to our target, and we see it at target in the medium term.

speaker: presidenta
text: And I would add one thing, because you didn't ask me, but, no, I'll wait until somebody

speaker: presidenta
text: asks me.

speaker: periodista
text: Oud Karzulek of BFM Business, please, Oud.
Good afternoon, and thank you for taking my question.
Under what conditions of inflation at a shooting would the ECB consider easing monetary policy?
How long and how far below 2%?
And on another subject, in the U.S., Kevin Walsh has been nominated to chair the Federal
Reserve.
Former central banker McCartney called it a fantastic choice.
Do you share that view, and have you worked with Mr. Walsh before?
Thank you.

speaker: presidenta
text: So, on Kevin Walsh, yes, I have known him for a long, long time, back in the financial

speaker: presidenta
text: crisis days, where he was in public service, and I was Minister of Finance at the time.

speaker: presidenta
text: So we go back a long way, and I very much welcome the announcement of his appointment.

speaker: presidenta
text: Now, I just want to take you back to the undershooting.

speaker: presidenta
text: We have projected undershooting in 2026 for a long time.

speaker: presidenta
text: And if you go back to our September projections, for instance, which were the last projections conducted by the ECB, we had actually this 1.7.

speaker: presidenta
text: and the 1.8% for the entire year.

speaker: presidenta
text: So this was changed and moved up in December.

speaker: presidenta
text: In a way, we are going back to the track that we had anticipated,

speaker: presidenta
text: and this is also what markets and economists are anticipating.

speaker: presidenta
text: But if you look at our medium-term target,

speaker: presidenta
text: which is what we rely upon,

speaker: presidenta
text: we are at 2% in 27, 2% in 28.

speaker: presidenta
text: I myself am particularly attentive, as you know,

speaker: presidenta
text: to services.

speaker: presidenta
text: Services is declining a little bit.

speaker: presidenta
text: I'm also very attentive as a result to wages.

speaker: presidenta
text: We have the wage cracker,

speaker: presidenta
text: which seems to guide us

speaker: presidenta
text: towards more growth moderation.

speaker: presidenta
text: We will have more data

speaker: presidenta
text: and intelligence coming out

speaker: presidenta
text: of the March exercise,

speaker: presidenta
text: but there is nothing

speaker: presidenta
text: that is really changing

speaker: presidenta
text: the baseline at all.

speaker: presidenta
text: And we, as I said, be looking at all data, not one single data point.

speaker: periodista
text: Olaf Storbeck of the Financial Times, please.
Thanks for taking my questions.
My first question is on kind of making sense of the mood music in the monetary policy statement.
Some analysts noted that it seems to have a bit of a hawkish subtext because you're kind of emphasising the positive elements
and kind of also emphasising that inflation is on track to meet your target.
Would you share that view that it's kind of more hawkish than dovish?
My second question is on core inflation,
which has fallen to, I think, the lowest level since October 2021
and is also below the ECB's Q1 forecast.
First, does the governing council see this as a good development, as it kind of suggests
inflation is coming down further and quicker than potentially expected, or is this seen
as a rather kind of negative trend because disinflation might be stronger than you want
it to be?
Thanks.

speaker: presidenta
text: Thank you for your two questions.

speaker: presidenta
text: So on your first question, I would like to mention that our monetary policy is in good

speaker: presidenta
text: shape.

speaker: presidenta
text: And it's in good shape because it is agile.

speaker: presidenta
text: And it is prepared to do what is necessary in order to reach our medium-term 2% targets

speaker: presidenta
text: in a symmetric way as we decided in our strategy assessment

speaker: presidenta
text: determination back in July 2025.

speaker: presidenta
text: So I'm not trying to characterize the hawkishness

speaker: presidenta
text: or the dovishness.

speaker: presidenta
text: This is something that you enjoy doing

speaker: presidenta
text: and that markets look at very attentively.

speaker: presidenta
text: But we are data dependent.

speaker: presidenta
text: We will decide meeting by meeting.

speaker: presidenta
text: We are not rate path predetermined.

speaker: presidenta
text: We do not give forward guidance.

speaker: presidenta
text: We are in this world of significant uncertainty

speaker: presidenta
text: where geopolitics, developments,

speaker: presidenta
text: determine a lot of developments.

speaker: presidenta
text: And that's what we're going to continue doing.

speaker: presidenta
text: Core inflation, you're right.

speaker: presidenta
text: It's one of the underlying inflation elements

speaker: presidenta
text: that we consider.

speaker: presidenta
text: That is one which has gone from 2.4 to 2.2.

speaker: presidenta
text: We're still at 2.2, by the way.

speaker: presidenta
text: And I think that it's following a path

speaker: presidenta
text: that we had anticipated, that we are pleased to see

speaker: presidenta
text: is taking us to targets.

speaker: presidenta
text: I would like to emphasize one element

speaker: presidenta
text: which you will allow me to pick up

speaker: presidenta
text: because I think it might be interesting.

speaker: presidenta
text: As you probably know, the leaders are meeting in a week's time to examine competitiveness,

speaker: presidenta
text: reforms and hopefully to accelerate the process.

speaker: presidenta
text: In our monetary policy statement, as you well know, we always have this paragraph, which

speaker: presidenta
text: has slightly evolved over the course of time, in which we welcome, we stress the urgent

speaker: presidenta
text: needs to strengthen the euro area and its economy in the present geopolitical context.

speaker: presidenta
text: You generally look at this paragraph and say, OK, it's still the same thing.

speaker: presidenta
text: So what we decided to do in anticipation of that meeting on the 12th of February is to

speaker: presidenta
text: actually give our checklist to the leaders.

speaker: presidenta
text: So I will send it to each of the leaders of the European Union, to the President of the
